title: Nationalism & Identity
hook: The belief that the world divides naturally into 'nations,' each deserving its own state, is one of the most powerful political forces of the last two centuries — for unity and for conflict.
key_points: Nationalism is the idea that a 'nation' is the natural political community, deserving self-rule.
A nation is a people sharing identity — language, culture, history — not just a state's territory.
It can unify and motivate self-determination, or fuel exclusion and conflict.
Identity politics more broadly organizes action around shared group identity.
content_html: Nationalism is the belief that humanity divides naturally into nations, and that the nation is the proper basis for political community — each entitled, in the strongest versions, to its own self-governing state. To grasp it, the key distinction is between a "nation" and a "state." A state is a political and territorial unit with a government; a nation is a people who feel they belong together through some shared combination of language, culture, history, religion, or ancestry. The nationalist aspiration is that the two should align — that each nation should govern itself in its own state — which is where the term "nation-state" comes from.
extra_html: Encyclopaedia Britannica describes nationalism as one of the most potent forces in modern history, and crucially a double-edged one. On the constructive side, it can forge solidarity among strangers, motivate people to sacrifice for a common good, and underpin the principle of self-determination — the claim of peoples to rule themselves rather than be ruled by empires or foreign powers, which drove decolonization and many independence movements. On the destructive side, defining an "us" bound by shared identity simultaneously defines a "them," and nationalism has fueled exclusion, persecution of minorities, xenophobia, and war. This is why it cuts across the usual left-right spectrum and attaches to very different movements. Nationalism is one expression of a broader phenomenon, identity politics, in which people organize and mobilize around a shared group identity — national, ethnic, religious, or other. Understanding it matters because the pull of identity helps explain political behavior that purely economic or ideological accounts miss: people are moved not only by what they want, but by who they believe they are.

related.title: Major Political Ideologies
related.hook: An ideology is a worldview about how society should be run — and a handful of them frame most political arguments you'll ever hear.

related.title: Populism
related.hook: Populism isn't a single program — it's a style that splits society into two camps: a virtuous 'people' against a corrupt 'elite,' with the populist speaking for the people.

related.title: Sovereignty Among Nations
related.hook: Inside its borders a state is supreme — but in the world of states there's no higher ruler. That gap, called anarchy, shapes everything about international politics.

flashcards.back_html: The idea that the nation — a people sharing identity, culture, and history — is the natural political community and deserves self-rule.

flashcards.prompt: How does a 'nation' differ from a 'state'?

choices.text: A nation is a people sharing identity; a state is a governing political unit over territory
They mean exactly the same thing
A nation is smaller than a city

flashcards.explanation_html: A nation is a community of shared identity; a state is the political and territorial apparatus — they don't always line up neatly.

flashcards.prompt: Why is nationalism described as double-edged?

choices.text: It can unify a people and justify self-determination, but also fuel exclusion and conflict
Because it has no effect on politics
Because it only ever causes peace

flashcards.explanation_html: The same sense of national belonging that binds people together can also define outsiders and drive conflict.
